title: The Hook
subtitle: MOUSE AIM · PROJECTILE · RETRIEVAL
description: Move the fire across the tiled void. Aim with the mouse and left-click to throw a chain hook at a freely floating ring. A catch reels the ring back to the fire, adds to the counter, and spawns another ring.
explanation: The game turns the mouse's 2D screen position into a 3D camera ray, then finds where that ray intersects a horizontal aiming plane. A left click launches the hook toward that world point. The hook has three simple states: idle, flying, and returning. While flying, the system checks the whole movement segment against the ring so a fast hook cannot skip over it between frames. On contact, the ring follows the hook back to the fire. At the fire, the ring is consumed, the counter increases, and a replacement ring appears at a new position.
algorithm: mouse screen point → camera ray → aim-plane point → hook flight → segment/ring collision → reel in → consume + count + respawn
learning_goals: Convert a 2D mouse position into a useful point in the 3D world with a camera ray and plane intersection.
Read a small state machine that moves the hook through idle, flying, and returning states.
Explain how frame time controls projectile speed and how segment collision avoids tunneling.
Trace how a caught ring is carried back, consumed, counted, and replaced.
review_points: Why does the cursor need a camera ray and an aiming plane before it can target a 3D position?
What prevents the hook from being launched again while it is already flying or returning?
Why test the segment from the previous hook position to the next one instead of only checking the endpoint?
At what moment does the counter increase, and what triggers the replacement ring?
Which components hold per-entity state, and which resource holds the shared catch count?
practice_tasks: Change the hook speed and catch radius, then compare how easy the ring is to catch.
Adjust the ring's bob and drift values. Try aiming ahead of a moving ring.
Change the number of chain links while keeping the hook flight speed the same.
Make the hook miss on purpose, then explain how it returns without changing the count.
Add a visual or sound cue when the hook changes from flying to returning.
